topics: batch size tradeoffs and tail latency
meeting_header: Date: 2026-01-24 UTC | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Ramos (Redwood) — Priya Patel, Luke Harmon, Monica D'Souza, Aaron Ng (StellarBank)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll get started, uh, quick agenda — cost run review, caching/batching experiments, next steps. Priya are you good on time?
[00:10] Priya Patel: Yep all good, thanks Maya. we pulled internal numbers from last 48 hours, saw some odd spikes in token burn.
[00:18] Diego Ramos: Cool, I have the run summary — i'll share screen after quick context. we ran the baseline with the r-mid model (note: transcription may say r-mid but it's our internal label), 512 context, batching target 32 but effective batch was 18 due to arrival spread.
[00:34] Luke Harmon: Quick Q: when you say tokens/sec/$ — how exactly are you normalizing? are we including infra overhead (eg, pre/post processing)?
[00:40] Maya Chen: Good call. we're normalizing raw generation tokens / GPU-dollar for the inference layer, excluding client-side pre/post. but Diego added a small overhead factor (~8%) to approximate infra pipeline.
[00:52] Diego Ramos: Right — actual numbers: baseline run tokens/sec per dollar for r-mid at current quantization was ~1,800 tks/$ for batch 18; when we artificially enforced batch 32 it went to ~2,400 tks/$ but p95 latency jumped from 210ms to 520ms.
[01:10] Monica D'Souza: That's a fairly big p95 jump — our product SLA wants p95 under 300ms for interactive flows.
[01:16] Priya Patel: Also noticed prefix cache saved ~22% tokens in chat sims where users re-use earlier system prompts and long contexts. Diego, is that KV cache or prefix?
[01:24] Diego Ramos: Good question. This run used prefix caching — basically we cache tokenized prefixes for cold-start paths. KV cache is more for stateful sessions across tokens, different tech. prefix cache reduced total generated tokens for our simulated user behavior from 100k to ~78k over the window.
[01:40] Aaron Ng: sorry jumping in late — for our auditors, can you confirm logs retention and whether request traces include user PII? security is a blocker for private data.
[01:48] Maya Chen: Short answer: we can configure no-PII logging. we'll attach SOC 2 and data retention docs in the follow-up.
[01:54] Diego Ramos: back to economics — we tried quantized variant (int8-ish run) which gave 15% improvement in tokens/$ but slightly higher variance on quality metrics. the 4-bit path we tested in lab gave 30% tokens/$ improvement but needs eval for hallucination regressions.
[02:12] Priya Patel: Hmm 4-bit is attractive for cost but we can't accept any quality regression for compliance reports. can we run targeted evals only on reporting prompts?
[02:22] Diego Ramos: yes, recommend two-step: targeted evals on your query set, then if pass, run a shadow 72-hr benchmark with traffic shape.
[02:30] Luke Harmon: About batching tradeoffs — we saw the mode where we hold at batch 32 gives best throughput but worst tail. any heuristics to auto-cutdown batch size under latency SLOs?
[02:38] Diego Ramos: We have adaptive batching: it will hold up to configured max batch but cut the hold window when queue latency would push p95 beyond SLO. we can tune hold window and max batch per route. in practice for your pattern i recommend max batch 24 with aggressive hold timeout (~8ms) to keep p95 < 300ms.
[02:58] Monica D'Souza: If we do that, how much tokens/$ do we lose?
[03:02] Diego Ramos: Roughly from the numbers: batch 18 baseline to batch 24 adaptive gives tokens/$ from 1,800 to ~2,100 (so about 16% improvement) while p95 stays ~280ms in our sim.
[03:14] Priya Patel: Great. Another variable is request-level caching — we had a lot of near-identical prompts from internal bots. can Redwood do dedupe caching at the proxy?
[03:22] Maya Chen: We do have an optional request fingerprinting layer to de-dup identical prompts; that would have saved another 6-9% in this run. we can turn it on for non-sensitive routes.
[03:32] Priya Patel: Cool. Also curious about route-level fallbacks — we need a cheaper fallback for high-traffic spikes, e.g., fallback to smaller model or cached answer. what's the MX for switching?
[03:40] Diego Ramos: You can configure router policy: route by latency SLA or cost. e.g., if primary is saturated, route 30% to a cheaper r-small variant that yields ~65% quality but holds latency. we observed 18% unit cost reduction with a 10% quality delta on our QA metrics.
[04:00] Luke Harmon: Regarding dedicated vs hosted — we're leaning private VPC for compliance. does dedicated give us better tokens/$ or is it mostly latency predictability?
[04:08] Maya Chen: Dedicated primarily gives predictability and lower unit cost at committed scale. unit economics improve with reserved capacity discounts. hosted is quicker to iterate. private on-prem is the highest control but ops overhead.
[04:20] Aaron Ng: For SOC2, we need KMS integration and audit logs. are these available for dedicated?
[04:26] Maya Chen: Yes — KMS integration, HSM bridging options, and per-request audit logs are available for dedicated/private. we'll attach the security docs link in the follow-up.
[04:36] Diego Ramos: Back to the experimental results — caching combined (prefix + dedupe) gave an effective 28-30% tokens saved; quantization int8 gave 15% improvement; batching tuned gave about 16% improvement; stacking them isn't perfectly additive due to overlap but we model 45% net improvement in tokens/$ in the best config.
[04:58] Priya Patel: That 45% is optimistic; i want to see the model with per-route breakdown. can you provide tokens/$ by route (reporting vs interactive vs internal bot)?
[05:06] Maya Chen: We'll provide per-route breakdown. Diego, we'll include spreadsheet columns for route, baseline tks/$, post-change tks/$, expected latency.
[05:14] Diego Ramos: Yep will do. Also note we saw one outlier run at midnight where effective batch fell to 6 because of traffic burst pattern, causing tokens/$ to drop dramatically; Luke we flagged an ingress throttling misconfiguration on your side that caused bursty arrivals — can you check?
[05:28] Luke Harmon: Ah yes, we have a cloud-front Lambda that batches events before forwarding — i'll check the config and share findings.
[05:34] Monica D'Souza: About the 72-hr benchmark — do you have a template for traffic shaping? we want to mimic business-hours spikes.
[05:40] Diego Ramos: We'll attach a small runner and traffic profile: 45% business-hours, 30% background batch, 25% burst events. we'll also include a scenario with cold sessions to exercise prefix caching.
[05:52] Priya Patel: On quality, when you tested 4-bit we saw slight hallucination drift on legal/regulatory prompts. is there an intermediate quant profile?
[05:58] Diego Ramos: There's mixed-precision and selective quant. we can quantize most layers to 4-bit but keep top layers in 8-bit — that often preserves quality while getting 20% cost savings vs full 8-bit.
[06:12] Maya Chen: We'll propose two quant profiles: conservative (selective) and aggressive (full 4-bit) and run your reporter prompts against both.
[06:20] Aaron Ng: Also, can we anonymize traces before we send to Redwood for debugging? privacy is a must.
[06:26] Maya Chen: Absolutely — redact at proxy and we'll only accept tokenless metadata if you prefer.
[06:32] Diego Ramos: Recap of actions — 1) Redwood sends batching + caching config + spreadsheet, 2) customer runs 72-hr shaped benchmark with prefix + dedupe on, 3) deep-dive on quantization with target prompts.
[06:44] Priya Patel: Sounds good. any other blockers from security?
[06:48] Aaron Ng: Mostly SOC2 docs and KMS details. i'll review the docs when you send them.
[06:54] Maya Chen: Great. we'll aim to drop everything by tuesday (2026-01-27). thanks everyone.
[07:02] Monica D'Souza: Thanks, bye.
[07:04] [meeting end — short notes omitted for brevity]
